Algerian Oil & Gas Sector Faces Disruption Amid Mediterranean Blockade

A major escalation in regional tensions has hit Algeria’s oil and gas industry, as naval forces from a neighboring country imposed a blockade on the port terminals at Skikda and Arzew late Tuesday night, halting crude and liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports. The move, described by the Algerian Ministry of Energy as “an unjustified act of aggression,” has already led to significant disruptions across the sector, with storage nearing capacity and upstream activity being curtailed.

Export operations at key terminals, including those run by El Mouradia Energy and SaharaPetro, ceased at 22:00 local time on June 25, according to an official at the Algerian Oil & Gas Producers Association. “We are unable to load tankers or send out shipments,” the official said. “The blockade has paralyzed our export capabilities, and if this continues for more than a week, the financial impact will be severe.”

Algeria is a major supplier of oil and gas to Southern Europe, exporting nearly 1.1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day. Analysts warn that continued obstruction could put upward pressure on global LNG prices and force domestic producers to scale back production due to limited storage capacity. “All upstream activity is now being re-evaluated,” said Lamine Benyahia, an energy markets analyst based in Algiers. “Producers like Atlas Hydrocarbons and North Sahara Gas have already begun to reduce output from key fields.”

The Algerian National Union of Oil & Gas Workers issued a statement expressing concern for the safety of workers at port facilities and urging authorities to secure sites. “Our members are facing a stressful situation with significant uncertainties,” said union spokesperson Amina Khelil. “We urge all parties to de-escalate and allow the safe passage of energy cargoes.”

As of Wednesday morning, satellite imagery confirmed at least seven fully loaded oil and LNG tankers stranded at anchor off the coast, unable to depart. The Ministry of Energy stated that, as of midday, combined losses for the sector exceeded $115 million in deferred shipments and demurrage costs.

Industry representatives are calling for urgent diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis. “The Algerian oil and gas sector is vital to both national revenues and international energy markets,” said Mohamed Larbi, president of the Oil & Gas Producers Association. “Extended disruption is not in the interest of any party.”

Talks to end the blockade have yet to yield a breakthrough, and sector officials warn the situation remains highly volatile.
